nameStory: Common cowparsnip gets its name because cattle love to graze on its large, nutritious leaves - though 'parsnip' refers to its carrot-family roots rather than the actual parsnip vegetable. Some folks call it 'Satan celery' because despite being in the same family as celery, this plant can cause nasty skin burns if you're not careful handling it.
description: Common cowparsnip is a towering native wildflower that can reach 6-10 feet tall, making it one of our most impressive roadside plants. It produces massive umbrella-shaped clusters of tiny white flowers perched atop thick, hollow stems. The huge compound leaves can be over a foot across, giving the whole plant a bold, tropical appearance that's hard to miss in New England's landscape.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large flat-topped umbels (umbrella-like clusters) of tiny white flowers, each cluster 6-12 inches across with an almost lacy appearance and a faint sweet scent

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Enormous compound leaves up to 18 inches wide, divided into 3 large maple-like leaflets that feel coarse and slightly fuzzy underneath

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Imposing height of 6-10 feet with thick, ridged, hollow stems that make a satisfying hollow thunk when tapped

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, oval seeds about half an inch long that develop in late summer, turning brown and papery with distinctive ridged wings

habitat: Look for cowparsnip in rich, moist soils along stream banks, forest edges, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It thrives in partially shaded areas where the soil stays consistently moist, often growing alongside other moisture-loving plants like jewelweed and wild ginger.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as reddish-purple stems with tightly furled leaves that gradually unfold into their massive mature size.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs from June through August, when the impressive white flower umbels are most showy and fragrant.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and turn brown while leaves begin to yellow, and the thick stems start to dry out but remain standing.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems persist as tall, hollow stalks that rattle in winter winds, while the plant dies back to its roots underground.

funFact: Despite being called 'Satan celery,' many Indigenous peoples of North America traditionally ate young cowparsnip stems and leaf stalks after careful preparation - the key was peeling away the outer skin and eating only the inner pith, which tastes surprisingly like celery!
confusionNotes: The biggest danger is confusing cowparsnip with its deadly relative, giant hogweed, which can cause severe burns and blindness. Remember: cowparsnip is usually 6-10 feet tall with green stems that may have purple spots, while giant hogweed towers up to 15 feet with stems covered in distinctive dark red or purple blotches and coarse hairs.
contextualKnowledge: This plant belongs to the carrot family (Apiaceae), the same family as carrots, celery, and parsley, but also deadly poison hemlock - which is why you should never eat any wild member of this family unless you're absolutely certain of its identity and proper preparation.
compareHints: Common cowparsnip is the only native North American member of the Heracleum genus, making it generally smaller and less dangerous than its introduced European cousins like giant hogweed. Unlike giant hogweed, our native cowparsnip has green stems (sometimes with purple spots) rather than the distinctive red-blotched, bristly stems of its more dangerous relative.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Giant hogweed dwarfs its relatives in the hogweed genus - while common cowparsnip reaches 3-6 feet with 6-inch flower clusters, giant hogweed towers at 8-15 feet with 2-foot flower umbels.
Compared to its North American cousin Common Cowparsnip, hogweed typically has more deeply divided leaves with narrower segments and slightly smaller flower clusters.
